newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin heart seen more diseased than expected.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin heart seen more diseased than expected.

text.p: Heart specialists said the greater than expected number of bypasses performed during heart surgery on Russian President Boris Yeltsin on Tuesday showed his heart was more badly diseased than previously thought.

"If you say you're going to do three or four bypasses and you do more, you've found more problems than you expected," said John Wright, head of cardiac services at the London Chest Hospital, Royal Hospitals Trust in London.
"The more bypasses, the more disease," Wright said.
The Russian surgeon who headed the seven-hour operation, Renat Akchurin, said his team had made "much more" than the expected three or four bypasses but declined to give a figure.
"The formal number of bypasses is not that important," Akchurin told a news conference in Moscow after the operation.
Wright said three bypasses was the average. "Above five is unusual. They will be patients with severe and diffused disease," he said.
Yeltsin's heart was stopped for 68 minutes during surgery.
"It's not an extraordinary long time but it's a significant amount of time," said Michael Rees, a professor at the Bristol Royal Infirmary in Britain.
He said of the greater number of bypasses: "It could lead to prolonged recuperation or complications in the future".
Akchurin said Yeltsin's lungs were on artificial ventilation. "This is normal and is usually done to prevent after-surgery complications," Akchurin said.
The London Chest Hospital's Wright said the "next landmark" for outsiders to watch for would be when Yeltsin was disconnected from the ventilator, which would be a good sign.

A report on the U.S. television network CBS on Monday quoted pioneering American heart surgeon Michael DeBakey, in Moscow to observe the operation, as saying that Yeltsin's heart was at one point only pumping 20 percent of the blood it should handle but was now working at around 50 percent.
The report said Yeltsin's right coronary artery was completely blocked and three other arteries partially blocked.
Meanwhile, a European cardiologist in Moscow, speaking on condition of anonymity, said multiple bypasses increased the risk of a further heart attack.
"If this is the case, there is all the chance of a new infarctus (heart attack) quickly," said the cardiologist.
